# Bidirekt

> Bidirekt is a declarative, static, bidirectional contract testing tool. Each participant (provider or consumer) writes a YAML contract declaring what it provides and what it consumes (a GraphQL provider publishes its GraphQL schema instead), publishes it to a broker with the `bidirekt` CLI, and asks `can-i-deploy` before deploying. Nothing is run: the broker compares declarations.

Workflow per participant, in this order: `create-participant` (once) → `validate` (before commit) → `publish` (every build) → `can-i-deploy` (before deploy) → deploy → `record-deployment` (after deploy succeeds).

## Setup

See it first: `curl -sL bidirekt.com/demo | sh` runs the petstore example with Docker, from a `can-i-deploy` break to the fixed version ([Demo](https://bidirekt.com/docs/start/demo.md)). Set up a project in one command: `curl -sL bidirekt.com/try | sh` downloads the broker's compose file to `bidirekt/compose.yaml`, installs the CLI and the agent skill, and prints the next steps, starting with `docker compose -f bidirekt/compose.yaml up -d` and opening `http://localhost:8080`, where the first access creates the admin with an email and a password ([Try on your project](https://bidirekt.com/docs/start/try.md)). The steps one by one:

Install the CLI (Linux and macOS, `x86_64` and `arm64`):

```
curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bidirekt/cli/v0.4.0/install.sh | sh
```

Prints `bidirekt 0.4.0 installed to ~/.local/bin/bidirekt`. To pin a version, pass it to the script: `sh -s -- v0.4.0`; `v` is optional.

Or with Homebrew (macOS and Linux): `brew tap bidirekt/tap`, `brew trust bidirekt/tap`, `brew install bidirekt`. The same tap has the broker as a service with your own Postgres: `brew install bidirekt-broker`, `createdb bidirekt`, `brew services start bidirekt-broker`; its settings are in `$(brew --prefix)/etc/bidirekt/broker.env`, written on the first start, and it listens on `http://localhost:8080`. The tap follows the releases within an hour of each one.

To upgrade the CLI, install the new release the way you installed it: run the install script again, `brew upgrade bidirekt`, or change the Docker tag. Upgrade the broker first; it migrates its database when it starts and a migration does not go back, so `pg_dump` the database before every upgrade. With Homebrew: `brew upgrade bidirekt-broker`, then `brew services restart bidirekt-broker`; with Docker or Docker Compose, change the image tag and start it again. `/health` shows the version running ([Run the broker: Upgrade](https://bidirekt.com/docs/start/run-the-broker.md#upgrade)).

Or run the CLI from its Docker image, `ghcr.io/bidirekt/cli:0.4.0` (`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`; each release is tagged only with its full version, no `latest`), with the project mounted and the broker and key in `BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL` and `BIDIREKT_API_KEY`: `docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work -e BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL=<url> -e BIDIREKT_API_KEY ghcr.io/bidirekt/cli:0.4.0 publish <file or folder>... --participant <name> --version <label>` (`-e BIDIREKT_API_KEY` passes the shell's value on). For the local compose's broker, add `--network host` and use `BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL=http://localhost:8080` (Linux and Docker Desktop on macOS).

Sign in to your broker, once per machine: create an API key on the broker's Profile page (`<broker>/profile/api-keys/new`, shown once), then run `bidirekt login` in a terminal; it asks for the profile, the broker URL and the key, and saves them:

```
bidirekt login
bidirekt login --profile local
```

A broker on a non-default profile (e.g. `--profile local` for the local compose) needs that profile on every command: `--profile local` or `export BIDIREKT_PROFILE=local`. In CI, or anywhere without a terminal, set `BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL` and `BIDIREKT_API_KEY` instead.

Install the agent skill that writes and fixes the contract files from the code (a TypeScript, JavaScript, PHP or Go service can instead generate its contract file from annotated code with the [TypeScript SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/typescript-sdk.md), the [PHP SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/php-sdk.md) or the [Go SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/go-sdk.md)):

```
npx skills add bidirekt/skills -a claude-code codex -y
```

Project install writes `.agents/skills/bidirekt/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/bidirekt` and `skills-lock.json` in the repo (`-a` picks the agents, `-y` skips the questions; `bidirekt.com/try` runs this same command). `-g` writes `~/.agents/skills/bidirekt/SKILL.md`, a link in each detected agent's skills folder (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/`) and `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json`; agents depend on what the `skills` tool detects. With `-g`, `✗ bidirekt → PromptScript: PromptScript does not support global skill installation` comes from the `skills` tool and can be ignored.

## Contract file

YAML, extension `.yaml` or `.yml`, one document per file; a GraphQL provider also passes its GraphQL schema files, `.graphql`, `.graphqls` or `.gql` (see `### graphql resources`). Three optional top-level keys, nothing else: `provides`, `consumes`, `schemas`. Participant name and version are CLI flags, never keys in the file. One file may carry both `provides` and `consumes`.

A TypeScript, JavaScript, PHP or Go service can instead write its contract from annotated code with the TypeScript SDK, the PHP SDK or the Go SDK: each SDK's `generate` command writes `contracts/generated.yaml`, which is then the service's contract file; a GraphQL subgraph's contract is that file plus its GraphQL schema, published and validated together (alone it fails with `graph "<graph>" without a GraphQL schema`). How to annotate the code is in [TypeScript SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/typescript-sdk.md), [PHP SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/php-sdk.md) and [Go SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/go-sdk.md).

```yaml
# provider petstore_api
provides:
  rest:
    /pets/*:
      get:
        responses:
          200: Pet
    /pets:
      post:
        request: NewPet
        responses:
          201: Pet
          400: Error

# consumer petstore_web: same rest block, nested under the provider's participant name
consumes:
  petstore_api:
    rest:
      /pets/*:
        get:
          responses:
            200: Pet

schemas:
  Pet:
    type: object
    properties:
      petId:
        type: integer
      name:
        type: string
      nickname:
        type: string
        optional: true
  Pets:
    type: array
    items:
      ref: Pet
```

Rules for every kind of resource:

- Resource = one body the two sides exchange; what identifies it depends on its kind. Kinds today: `rest` (a provider writes `provides.rest`, a consumer `consumes.<provider>.rest`) and `graphql` (a provider publishes its GraphQL schema, a consumer writes `consumes.<provider>.graphql`). Each resource is compared on its own.
- Every body a resource declares names a schema declared under `schemas`, never an inline schema, or is `~` = body not described: nothing in it is compared, the resource still exists. On the producing side `~` promises no structure; on the reading side it reads nothing. `""` is an unresolved schema name, not `~`.
- Consumer key under `consumes` = the provider's participant name, snake_case, or a GraphQL graph name. Not checked at publish: a typo publishes and fails at `can-i-deploy` with "is not deployed in <env>".
- Schema node `type`: `object`, `array`, `map`, `enum`, `union`, `string`, `integer`, `float`, `number`, `boolean`, and `scalar` (GraphQL custom scalar, `type: scalar` + `name: DateTime`; in a schema a REST resource reaches → `type "scalar" is only allowed in GraphQL contracts at <path>`). No `format`: an unknown key, rejected at publish (`unknown key "format" at schemas Pet properties birthDate`). Enum values are `type: enum` + `members`, never an `enum` key beside `type: string` (also unknown). `integer` ≠ `float`, both strict. A `number` reader accepts an `integer`, `float` or `number` producer; a `number` producer breaks an `integer` or `float` reader (JSON sends `50` for a round float: read it as `number`; a producer whose value can be a round float writes `number` too, e.g. PHP `json_encode` sends `50.0` as `50`).
- Each type takes only its own key: `properties` on `object` (at least one), `items` on `array` (required), `values` on `map` (required), `members` on `enum` and `union` (required), none on a primitive; a key on another type → `"items" is not allowed on a string schema at <path>, use it with "type: array"` (`properties` → `object`, `items` → `array`, `values` → `map`, `members` → `use it with "type: enum" or "type: union"`). Every node declares `type`, except a `ref`; neither → `missing "type" at <path>, expected one of: object, array, map, string, integer, float, number, boolean, enum, union, scalar`. `name` on a type other than `scalar` → `"name" is not allowed on an object schema at <path>, use it with "type: scalar" (GraphQL contracts only)`.
- `object` without `properties`, or with `properties: {}` → `object schema without properties at <path>, declare the keys you read, or use "type: map" with "values" if the keys vary`: declare the keys that arrive in the body (a fixed key with a reserved character in its name stays out, see property and schema names below). The reader marks each key its code doesn't read `optional: true` (e.g. the item keys of an array it only counts), so the producer may drop it; the producer declares the keys it sends. Varying keys → `map` with `values` on both sides.
- Map (dynamic keys, all values one shape): `type: map` + `values: <node>`, e.g. `PetsByName: {type: map, values: {ref: Pet}}` for `{"bob": {...}, "sky": {...}}`. Keys are strings. No `values` → `map schema without values at <path>`. `type: object` + `values` without `properties` → two lines at the same path, `"values" is not allowed on an object schema at <path>, use it with "type: map"` then `object schema without properties at <path>, …`: write `type: map`. A map only matches a map: values compare like array items; the key is the path segment `{}` (`$.pets{}.name`), the type prints `map<T>`. Map against `object` (either side, in any body) = one type mismatch on the property (`Owner.pets — petstore_api provides it as object, but petstore_web reads map<object>`), nothing inside compared; fix: the same shape on both sides (fixed keys → `object` with `properties`, except a key with a reserved character, left out; varying keys → `map`).
- Enum (a string from a fixed list): `type: enum` + `members`, a non-empty list of non-empty strings, none repeated, e.g. `status: {type: enum, members: [available, pending, sold]}`. Strings only: one of a few numbers is an `integer`. Values are data, not names: any character except NUL, never part of a path. `optional`/`nullable` as on any property. Rejected at publish:
  - no `members` → `"type: enum" needs "members" at schemas Pet properties status: list its values`
  - `members: []` → `"members" is empty at schemas Pet properties status: list at least one value`
  - a value twice → `value "sold" is repeated in "members" at schemas Pet properties status`
  - a value that is not a string, is empty, or holds NUL → `each value in "members" must be non-empty text at schemas Pet properties status`
- Union (one of several named schemas): `type: union` + `members`, a non-empty map from each member key to a node with only `ref`, e.g. `payment: {type: union, members: {card: {ref: CardPayment}, cash: {ref: CashPayment}}}`. The key is the member's identity on the wire (REST: the value of the field that tells the members apart, e.g. `"method": "card"`). No `discriminator`: when the code reads that field, it is a plain property of each member's schema. (GraphQL: the key is the type name, and a union may also carry `properties` to read an interface; see `### graphql resources`.) A member is the path segment `(<key>)`: `$.payment(card).number`, field `Order.payment(card)`; a union that is the whole schema `Payment` → `Payment(card)`. Rejected at publish:
  - no `members` → `"type: union" needs "members" at schemas Order properties payment: map each key to a ref`
  - `members: {}` → `"members" is empty at schemas Order properties payment: list at least one member`
  - a member without `ref` → `member "card" needs a "ref" to a schema at schemas Order properties payment`
  - a member key with a reserved character → `member key "card(x)" must not contain ".", "[", "]", "{", "}", ";", "(" or ")" at schemas Order properties payment`
  - any other key in a member (e.g. `type`) → unknown key; a member `ref` no schema declares → unresolved ref, as any `ref`.
- Enum and union compare by the two core rules (below). The reader decides: a `string` reader accepts an `enum` producer; an `enum` reader against a `string` producer is a type mismatch; an enum against any other type, or a union against anything but a union, is a type mismatch (types print `enum`/`union`, never their values). The provider owns how a property is provided: every enum value and union member the consumer declares must be declared by the provider, whichever side produces the body; a value or member only the provider declares never breaks. Consumer request `[available, sold]` vs provider `[available, pending]` breaks on `sold`; consumer response `[available, adopted]` vs provider `[available, pending]` breaks on `adopted`; consumer `[available]` vs provider `[available, pending]` is compatible in either body. Two unions: each consumer member key must exist in the provider, and a member on both sides compares as any schema (a property inside breaks as a property, at `$.payment(card).number`).
- Properties are required unless `optional: true` (the key may be missing). There is no `required` list. `nullable: true` (any node but a union member: property, `items`, `values`, root) = the key is there and the value may be `null`; independent of `optional`.
- `optional` only on a property (with or without `ref` beside it). On `items`, `values` or a named schema it is rejected, `optional: false` too:
  - `"optional" is not allowed on array items at schemas Pet properties tags items, mark the property that holds the array optional, or use "nullable: true" for an item that may be null`
  - `"optional" is not allowed on map values at schemas Pet properties scores values, mark the property that holds the map optional, or use "nullable: true" for a value that may be null`
  - `"optional" is not allowed on a schema at schemas Pet, mark optional the property that uses it, beside its "ref"`
- Modeling null and absence: write what the code does, not the type it declares (a nullable type the code never sets to `null` gets no `nullable`). With the TypeScript SDK, the PHP SDK or the Go SDK, a field's declared `type`, `optional` or `nullable` applies this rule over its TypeScript, PHP or Go type (Describe what the code does, in [TypeScript SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/typescript-sdk.md#describe-what-the-code-does), [PHP SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/php-sdk.md#describe-what-the-code-does) and [Go SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/go-sdk.md#describe-what-the-code-does)). The reader writes the flags from how its code reads each property, the producer from what its code can send (which side produces and which reads depends on the resource; `rest`: see below):
  - Reader, per property: if this value comes `null` or is missing, does the code keep working? Keeps working with `null` → `nullable: true`; keeps working without the key → `optional: true`; breaks → neither.
  - Producer: may send `null` → `nullable: true`; may leave the key out → `optional: true`.
  - A provider that reads a body marks a property by what it accepts without answering an error. A missing `name` answered with `400` → `name` is required.
- A schema no resource, `ref` or `arguments` names is accepted and never compared; a file with only `schemas` is valid.
- `ref: <SchemaName>` reuses a named schema at any depth; allowed beside it: only `nullable`, `description` (ASCII letters and digits, a single space between words), and `optional` when the node is a property (`nullable` makes the node nullable, `optional` the property optional, even when the named schema is not); a union member is its `ref` alone. `type`/`properties`/`items`/`values` beside it is rejected (`"type" is not allowed beside "ref" at schemas Pet properties owner`): keep the `ref` alone or the shape without it, whichever describes the body. Unknown `ref` is rejected.
- Recursion is allowed through a property, an item or a value: a schema may reach itself directly or indirectly (`Comment.replies[] → Comment`, `Post.author → User` / `User.posts[] → Post`). No depth limit. A schema that only refers to itself through `ref`, with no type on the way (`A: {ref: B}`, `B: {ref: A}`), is rejected: `schema "A" only refers to itself through ref (A → B → A): give one of them a type`.
- `description` is allowed on any node but a union member, and never compared. It holds ASCII letters and digits, with a single space between words (`In kilograms`). Anything else (punctuation, accents, a line break, two spaces) is rejected at publish with `schema.description_syntax`: `invalid description "In kilograms." at schemas Pet properties weight, must be ASCII letters and digits, with single spaces between words`; an empty one ends with `must not be empty`.
- Every unknown key at any level is a violation (`options`, `GET`, top-level `version`, an `enum` key, `format`). YAML anchors/aliases are rejected; comments are allowed.
- Property and schema names, and union member keys: not empty (`must not be empty`), no `.`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `;`, `(` or `)` (reserved for the paths the broker compares and shows: `$.owner.name`, `$[].photoUrl`, `$.pets{}.name`, `$.payment(card).number`), no control characters (`must not contain control characters`). Anything else is valid (`content-type`, `@type`, `$ref`, `first name`):
  - `invalid property name "user.name" at schemas Pet properties, must not contain ".", "[", "]", "{", "}", ";", "(" or ")"`
  - `invalid schema name "Pet.v2" at schemas, must not contain ".", "[", "]", "{", "}", ";", "(" or ")"`
  - `member key "card(x)" must not contain ".", "[", "]", "{", "}", ";", "(" or ")" at schemas Order properties payment`
  - Fix: rename the schema (the name lives only in the contract); a property name that is a typo → rename it to the key the body really has; a fixed key the body really has with one of these characters → leave it out of the contract (an undeclared property is not checked); varying keys → `map` (its keys are not property names).
- Declare only what you use: a consumer lists only the properties it reads or sends; the provider may drop anything else.

Several files: all files of one `publish` are one contract, order irrelevant.

- Schema names are one namespace across files; the same name twice is a duplicate. The types of a GraphQL schema are a namespace of their own: a YAML `Pet` and a GraphQL `type Pet` never collide.
- Provider: each resource declared in exactly one file (its resources may be split across files). A file reached twice (passed twice, or passed and also inside a passed folder) is read once, not a duplicate.
- Consumer: fragments of the same resource merge by union. In a body the consumer reads: a property is optional only if every fragment that declares it marks it optional, nullable only if every fragment that declares it accepts `null`; a fragment that doesn't declare the property or its parent doesn't count. In a body the consumer produces: required only if every fragment that declares its parent sends it, nullable if any fragment may send `null`; a fragment that omits the parent too makes only the parent optional. A fragment with `~` for the body: in a body the consumer reads it adds nothing; in a body the consumer produces it makes the body itself optional (a provider that requires the body breaks with `sends it only sometimes`). Every fragment `~` = no body, as with one `~`. Different types for one property (even `number` vs `integer`) are rejected at publish, and so are two enums with different values: `conflicting values for property "$.status" of <resource>: [a, b] here, [a, c] in other.yaml`. The members of a union join by union, like properties (`card` in one fragment, `card` and `cash` in another → both).

Rejected at publish, so never compared: `format` and an `enum` key, both unknown keys (a `string` is any string). Accepted and compared: `type: enum` with its `members`. Not compared (never breaks): `description` (its text is checked at publish: ASCII letters and digits, a single space between words), a property the reader does not declare, a schema no resource or `ref` names, an enum value or union member only the provider declares.

### `rest` resources

- REST resource = the request of (endpoint, method), or one response of (endpoint, method, status). The consumer produces a request and the provider reads it; the provider produces a response and the consumer reads it. A report names it `<METHOD> <endpoint> request` or `<METHOD> <endpoint> response <status>`.
- Methods: `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, lowercase only. `request` only on `post`, `put` and `patch`. A method may have only `request`, only `responses`, or both.
- `~` (or no value, `204:`) for a body not described. A file or multipart body is `~`, in a request or a response. Provider `200: ~` vs consumer `200: Pet` breaks once, on the body; provider `200: Pet` vs consumer `200: ~` and provider `request: ~` vs consumer `request: NewFile` are compatible.
- Status: integer 100–599, quoted or not. No patterns (`2xx` rejected).
- Which statuses: a consumer declares a status when its code does something specific with it or reads its body (generic "any error" handling doesn't count); a provider declares the statuses its code actually returns (a branch that never runs is left out). A consumer's status must exist in the provider; a provider-only status obliges no one.
- Endpoint: dynamic segment = `*`, one per segment (`/pets/*`, `/owners/*/pets/*`). Any other form is rejected at publish: `/pets/{petId}`, `/pets/:petId`, `/pets/<petId>`, `/pets/[petId]`, `/pets/p*` → `dynamic path segments must use *` (when each dynamic segment is one whole parameter, the report also gives the endpoint to write: `write "/pets/*"`); `/pets//photos`, `/pets;v=2`, `/pets/a b` → `malformed path`. Trailing slash is removed (`/pets/` = `/pets`). Consumer and provider endpoints match only when written identically.
- Several files: a provider's files may split endpoints, methods or even the statuses of one method between them; the `request` of an endpoint+method lives in one file only.
- Not compared: headers, query parameters. The `rest` block has no key for them; a `headers` key is rejected as unknown.

### `graphql` resources

- GraphQL resource = for each field of the query or mutation root, its `arguments` (produced by the consumer, read by the provider) and its `returns` (produced by the provider, read by the consumer). A report names it `query pet`, with places `query pet returns at "<p>"` or `query pet arguments (argument "<a>")`.
- Provider: publishes the GraphQL schema its application has, `.graphql`/`.graphqls`/`.gql`, no YAML needed: `bidirekt publish schema.graphqls --participant petstore_api --version 1.4.0`. All schema files of one publish are one schema (types in one file, `Query` in another). Every field of `Query`/`Mutation` (or the roots `schema { … }` names) is a provided resource; `Subscription` is ignored. `provides.graphql` takes only `graph` (subgraphs); `query`/`mutation` there are unknown keys. Invalid GraphQL → `cannot post contract to broker: <file>:<line>:<col>: <message>` (`./api/query.graphqls:2:17: Undefined type Pet.`; `query.graphqls:1:13: Cannot extend type "Query" because it is not defined.` outside a subgraph); a client operations file → `./operations.graphql: holds client operations; publish expects the GraphQL schema`.
- Consumer: `consumes.<provider>.graphql.query|mutation.<field>: {arguments: <Schema>, returns: <Schema>}`, the field's name alone as key (`invalid GraphQL field name "pets(first: 10)" at consumes petstore_api graphql query, write the field name only; arguments go in "arguments"`). `returns` required (`missing "returns" at consumes petstore_api graphql query pet`). No `arguments` = sends none, so a new required argument breaks it. `arguments` names a non-nullable object schema (`"arguments" must name an object schema at <path>: PetId is string`, `"arguments" must name a non-nullable schema at <path>: MaybeArgs is nullable`). Top nullability/list live in the named schema: `MaybePet: {ref: Pet, nullable: true}` for `pet: Pet`, `PetList: {type: array, items: {ref: Pet}}` for `[Pet!]!`. Declare only the selected fields. A nested field with arguments: `reviews: {type: array, items: {ref: Review}, arguments: ReviewsArgs}` (only on a property; in a schema a REST resource reaches → `"arguments" is only allowed in GraphQL contracts at <path>`). `subscription`, and `graph` under `consumes`, are unknown keys. Root fields starting with `__` (introspection) are dropped; `__typename` always passes.
- Mapping: `String`/`ID` → `string`, `Int` → `integer`, `Float` → `float` (read it as `number` to accept any number), `Boolean` → `boolean`, `scalar DateTime` → `{type: scalar, name: DateTime}` (matches by name; without `name` → `scalar schema without name at <path>`), `type`/`input` → `object`, `enum` → `enum`, `union` → `union` keyed by type names, `interface` → read as an object (its fields), as a union of its implementations, or both: `{type: union, properties: {id: …}, members: {User: {ref: UserName}}}` (union with `properties` is GraphQL only). Output field without `!` = `nullable`, never `optional`; argument/input field without `!` = `optional` + `nullable`; with `!` and a default = `optional`.
- Comparison on top of the core rule: a field the consumer reads must exist, even if `optional`; input is closed (an argument or input field the provider doesn't declare breaks, even optional); output non-null→nullable breaks a reader; argument nullable→non-null breaks a sender that may send null; new required argument breaks; input coercion: `integer`/`number` → `Float`, `integer` → `ID`, a single value → a list pass, `integer` → `String` breaks; a provider candidate that changes the named type of an argument a deployed consumer sends (`ID`→`String`, renamed input/enum) breaks it, in the provider's check only; output type names are not compared. A `Float`→`Int` output change breaks a consumer reading `float`, not one reading `number`.
- Not compared: descriptions, default values, directives that are behavior (custom, `@authenticated`, `@requiresScopes`, `@policy`, `@deprecated`, `@specifiedBy`), subscriptions, `@oneOf` (read as a plain input, the one-member rule unchecked), the client's operations (`@defer`, `@stream`, fragments), introspection.
- Graph (Apollo Federation 2): a subgraph publishes its schema with the federation `@link` plus a YAML `provides: {graphql: {graph: petstore_graph}}` in the same command (`bidirekt publish graph.yaml schema.graphqls …`). The graph is only a name, not a participant; consumers write `consumes.petstore_graph.graphql…` and are compared with the graph composed from the subgraphs deployed in the environment. Errors: `graph "petstore_graph" without a GraphQL schema at provides graphql, pass its .graphql, .graphqls or .gql in the same command`; `the GraphQL schema links Apollo Federation, but no graph is declared, declare it in provides.graphql.graph`; `invalid graph name "Petstore-Graph" at provides graphql, must be snake_case`; `graph name "petstore_graph" is already a participant name at provides graphql, pick another graph name`; `graph "other_graph" conflicts with graph "petstore_graph" declared in contracts/api.yaml at provides graphql, a contract belongs to one graph: declare the same name in every file`. A subgraph's check compares each deployed consumer of the graph with the graph composed with the candidate and reports only the breaks the candidate causes, written `<subgraph> (via <graph>) …`. Composition counts only `@key`, `@shareable`, `@inaccessible`, `@external`, `@override` (`from` = a participant name), `@provides`, `@interfaceObject`; errors such as `petstore_api 1.4.0 and petstore_reviews 2.0.0 both resolve Pet.name without @shareable`. Not checked: `@requires`/`@provides` field rules, `@external` rules, some `@inaccessible` rules, default mismatches, interface keys, `NO_QUERIES`, `SHAREABLE_HAS_MISMATCHED_RUNTIME_TYPES`, an implementation re-declaring an `@interfaceObject` field. One shape Apollo composes fails here: a shared field returning a union in one subgraph and one member in another, where a field of the other member lives only in the second subgraph with no `@key` to reach it. `/graphs/<name>` in the web UI shows each environment's deployed subgraphs and composition errors; it composes only deployed subgraphs, so a candidate's error from a subgraph check doesn't show there.

## CLI

Every broker command needs a broker URL and an API key; there is no default. Resolution: `BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL` and `BIDIREKT_API_KEY`, both set → else the active profile's saved URL and key. Set both variables or neither; only one fails with `set both BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL and BIDIREKT_API_KEY, or neither`. Active profile: `--profile` → `BIDIREKT_PROFILE` → `default`. With no URL: `no broker configured — run "bidirekt login" or set BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL and BIDIREKT_API_KEY`, plus, when the config file has other profiles, `the config file has the profile local — pass --profile local or set BIDIREKT_PROFILE=local` (several: `the config file has the profiles acme, local — pass --profile <name> or set BIDIREKT_PROFILE=<name>`). `--profile` goes before or after the command. In CI, set `BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL` and `BIDIREKT_API_KEY`. A key always starts with `bdk_`: `the API key from BIDIREKT_API_KEY doesn't start with bdk_` (or `the API key in profile <name> doesn't start with bdk_`). Broker refusals, on any command: 401 → `not signed in to <url> — run "bidirekt login" or set BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL and BIDIREKT_API_KEY` (key revoked, expired, its user deactivated, or a profile without a key); 403 → `the API key can't do this — check its permission at <url>/profile` (a `read` key can only list, `validate` and `can-i-deploy`; `write` adds `create-participant`, `create-environment`, `publish` and `record-deployment`); 426 → `bidirekt <version> doesn't work with this broker (<broker version>); upgrade bidirekt to <minimum version> or later` (install that version or newer). A report with breaks of a protocol the CLI doesn't know stops with exit 1: `the broker reported protocol <key>, which this bidirekt doesn't know; update bidirekt`.

- `bidirekt login [--profile <name>]` — asks for the profile (when `--profile` is not given), the broker URL and the API key (not echoed), checks the key with the broker, and only then saves URL and key in `~/.config/bidirekt/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bidirekt/config.json`, or `BIDIREKT_CONFIG_FILE`), readable only by you: `{"profiles": {"acme": {"brokerUrl": "https://broker.acme.example", "apiKey": "bdk_…"}}}`. Prints `Signed in to <url> as profile <name>`. URL must be `http://` or `https://` plus a host. Errors: `an API key starts with bdk_`, `the broker refused this API key`, `cannot reach the broker at <url>: <reason>`; outside a terminal (stdin from `/dev/null` included) `no terminal to sign in — set BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL and BIDIREKT_API_KEY`. Replacing a key warns `the previous key is still valid — revoke it at <url>/profile`. One profile per broker (account), never per environment.
- `bidirekt logout [--profile <name>]` — removes the key from the profile (the URL stays), without calling the broker: `Signed out of <url> (profile <name>). The key is still valid — revoke it at <url>/profile`; a profile without a key prints `not signed in on profile <name>`.
- `bidirekt create-participant <name>` — name in snake_case (`cannot post participant to broker: participant name must be snake_case`). Idempotent: an existing name prints `<name> participant already exists` and exits 0. The name can't change once created; a wrong name means creating another participant. A GraphQL graph name is refused, exit 1: `cannot post participant to broker: "petstore_graph" is a graph name; pick another participant name`.
- `bidirekt create-environment <name>` — e.g. `production`. Idempotent.
- `bidirekt validate <file or folder>... [--participant <name> --environment <env>]` — reads files and folders and checks them as `publish` does. Nothing is stored. Without the two flags it checks only the files: valid → `contract is valid; add --participant and --environment to compare it with what is deployed` on stdout, exit 0; violations print as in `publish`, on stderr, exit 1. With both, it then compares them with every counterpart deployed in `<env>`, as `can-i-deploy` does. Exit 0 = yes, exit 1 = no; the report goes to stdout either way (after the stderr `Broker:` line), starts with `<participant> local contract can be deployed to <env>` or `<participant> local contract cannot be deployed to <env>`, and carries the same lines as `can-i-deploy` (see `## Fixing can-i-deploy breaks`). Violations print as in `publish`. Participant and environment are checked before any file: `participant "<name>" not found → create it with: bidirekt create-participant <name>`, `cannot validate contract on broker: environment not found`. The two flags go together, and both refusals come before calling the broker: only one fails with `if any flags in the group [participant environment] are set they must all be set; missing [environment]` (or `missing [participant]`), an empty value with `--environment cannot be empty` (or `--participant cannot be empty`).
- `bidirekt publish <file or folder>... --participant <name> --version <label>` — all files publish together as one contract. A folder = every `.yaml`/`.yml`/`.graphql`/`.graphqls`/`.gql` file under it, subfolders included, other files ignored; a folder with none fails with `no contract files (.yaml, .yml, .graphql, .graphqls, .gql) in folder: "<folder>"`. Every GraphQL file in a folder is published as the participant's schema: a file of client queries or fragments fails with `<file>: holds client operations; publish expects the GraphQL schema`, and a third-party schema kept there would be published as the participant's own API. Files and folders mix in one command; the files go in alphabetical order, and a file reached twice is read once, named as the first argument that reached it. A file found in a folder is named by the folder plus its path inside it, without a leading `./` (`./contracts/` → `contracts/rest/pets.yaml`); a file passed directly keeps its name as typed. Participant must exist, checked before any file (`participant "<name>" not found → create it with: bidirekt create-participant <name>`). One request carries at most 8 MiB, the text of every file included (`validate` too); a larger one is refused before any file is checked. Same version with different content fails (`cannot post contract to broker: contract version already exists with different content`); versions are immutable, so commit the contract files first and publish from that commit (a hash taken before the files are committed names code that doesn't hold them). Any spec violation rejects the whole publish. Two steps: first each file's shape (keys, resources, schema nodes), every shape violation printed; only when all files pass, the checks between names (duplicate resources or schemas, one consumer property with two types or two lists of enum values, unresolved schema names). A file with a shape violation shows only that until it is fixed; the next run shows the rest:
  ```
  contract validation failed
    - petstore_api.yaml: invalid endpoint "/pets/{petId}" in provides, write "/pets/*" (dynamic path segments must use *)
  ```
- `bidirekt can-i-deploy <participant> --version <v> --environment <env>` — exit 0 = yes, exit 1 = no; the report goes to stdout either way. A yes (here and in `validate`) prints a second line naming what it compared with, alphabetically:
  ```
  petstore_web 2.3.0 can be deployed to production
  compared with: petstore_api, petstore_reviews
  ```
  or `nothing deployed in production to compare with` when no counterpart is deployed there (a vacuous yes). Errors, checked in this order: `cannot query can-i-deploy from broker: participant not found`, `cannot query can-i-deploy from broker: contract not found` (version never published), `cannot query can-i-deploy from broker: environment not found`.
- `bidirekt record-deployment <participant> --version <v> --environment <env>` — run after a successful deploy. Never blocks. Prints `<participant> deployment recorded to <env>`. Recording a version that was deployed in `<env>` before and is not the current one there is a rollback, and prints `<participant> rolled back to <version> in <env>`.
- `bidirekt list-participants` — prints every participant name, one per line on stdout, in alphabetical order; nothing when there are none, exit 0. Check names here before writing `consumes` (a graph is not a participant and is not listed).
- `bidirekt list-environments` — prints every environment name, one per line on stdout, in alphabetical order; nothing when there are none, exit 0. Check names here before passing `--environment`.
- `bidirekt version` (or `--version`, `-v`).

Every broker command first prints `Broker: <url> (<source>)` on stderr (`(profile: default)`, `(from BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL)`), on success too; stdout output comes after it. An `http://` URL on a host other than `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` adds `warning: the API key travels unencrypted to <url>` on stderr, and the command goes on.

Exit codes: 0 on success, help and version; 1 for everything else. Success goes to stdout, failures to stderr, except the `can-i-deploy` and `validate` reports (always stdout) and the `Broker:` line (always stderr).

## Fixing can-i-deploy breaks

Report shape: `<participant> <version> cannot be deployed to <env>`, then one block per incompatible counterpart. In it, first the breaks of a resource, under the resource, one break per line, each followed by its fix lines (`rest`: see below). Then the property breaks, one block per field, break and fix, sorted by field: the header `<f> — <break>` (plus ` (<N> places)` when there is more than one place), its fix lines once, then one place line per resource and path where it happens, `· <resource> at "<p>"` (`rest`: `<METHOD> <endpoint> request` or `<METHOD> <endpoint> response <s>`), ending with ` (<c>: <cf>)` (the counterpart's own field) when the counterpart has one there. `<f>` is the field of the participant under check: schema name + path inside that schema (`Owner.address.city`, `Pet.vaccinations[].name` for array items, `PetsByName{}.name` for map values, `Order.payment(card)` for the union member `card`, `Payment(card)` when the union is the whole schema, only `Pet` at the root). That is the schema to edit in its contract. When that participant has no field there (the `doesn't provide it, but` and `doesn't send it, but` breaks), `<f>` is the counterpart's field; for a missing enum value or union member (`doesn't provide "<m>", but`), `<f>` stays the participant's own field, since both sides declare the property. `<p>` is a path from the body root: `$.owner.name`, `$[].photoUrl` (array items), `$.pets{}.name` (map values), `$.payment(card).number` (inside the union member `card`); the root prints as `the body`, unquoted. Types print `array<T>` and `map<T>`; an enum prints `enum` and a union `union`, without their values (`graphql`: see below, types print as GraphQL writes them). A graph counterpart's header names its deployed subgraphs: `petstore_graph (petstore_api 1.4.0 + petstore_reviews 2.0.0, deployed):`. A difference inside a schema used in several places is one block, with one place per resource that reaches it, each with one of the paths that reach it there; a block holds only bodies the provider produces or only bodies the consumer produces, so the same difference in one of each is two blocks:
  ```
  petstore_api (1.4.0, deployed):
    POST /pets/*/adopt
      response 200:
        - petstore_web reads response 200, but petstore_api answers only 204
          → petstore_web: read response 204
          → petstore_api: answer 200
    Pet.status — petstore_web reads it, but petstore_api doesn't provide it (2 places)
      → petstore_web: stop reading it, or handle its absence in the code and mark it optional
      → petstore_api: provide it
        · GET /pets response 200 at "$[].status"
        · GET /pets/* response 200 at "$.status"
    Pet.weight — petstore_web reads it as string, but petstore_api provides float (2 places)
      → petstore_web: read it as float
      → petstore_api: provide it as string there
        · GET /pets response 200 at "$[].weight" (petstore_api: Pet.weight)
        · GET /pets/* response 200 at "$.weight" (petstore_api: Pet.weight)
  ```
Below each break come its fixes, one line per side, the participant under check first: `→ <participant>: <fix>`, then `→ <c>: <fix>`, which in a block ends with ` there` when the places name `<cf>`. A fix is a code change first, then the contract change that matches it: the contract follows the code. Each property break, with the fix of the participant under check, then `<c>`'s:

- `reads it, but <c> doesn't provide it` → `stop reading it, or handle its absence in the code and mark it optional`; <c>: `provide it`.
- `doesn't provide it, but <c> reads it` → `provide it`; <c>: `stop reading it, or handle its absence in the code and mark it optional there`.
- `requires it, but <c> only sometimes provides it` → `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional`; <c>: `always provide it there`.
- `provides it only sometimes, but <c> requires it` → `always provide it`; <c>: `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional there`.
- `doesn't send it, but <c> requires it` → `send it`; <c>: `stop requiring it, then mark it optional there`.
- `requires it, but <c> doesn't send it` → `stop requiring it, then mark it optional`; <c>: `send it`.
- `sends it only sometimes, but <c> requires it` → `always send it`; <c>: `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional there`.
- `requires it, but <c> sends it only sometimes` → `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional`; <c>: `always send it there`.
- `reads it as <t>, but <c> provides <t2>` → `read it as <t2>`; <c>: `provide it as <t> there`.
- `provides it as <t>, but <c> reads <t2>` → `provide it as <t2>`; <c>: `read it as <t> there`.
- `sends it as <t>, but <c> expects <t2>` → `send <t2>`; <c>: `accept <t> there`.
- `expects it as <t>, but <c> sends <t2>` → `accept <t2>`; <c>: `send <t> there`.
- `doesn't accept null, but <c> may provide null` → `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable`; <c>: `stop providing null there`.
- `may provide null, but <c> doesn't accept it` → `stop providing null`; <c>: `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable there`.
- `may send null, but <c> doesn't accept it` → `stop sending null`; <c>: `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable there`.
- `doesn't accept null, but <c> may send it` → `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable`; <c>: `stop sending null there`.
- `reads "<m>", but <c> doesn't provide it` → `stop reading "<m>"`; <c>: `provide "<m>" there`.
- `doesn't provide "<m>", but <c> reads it` → `provide "<m>"`; <c>: `stop reading "<m>" there`.
- `sends "<m>", but <c> doesn't accept it` → `stop sending "<m>"`; <c>: `accept "<m>" there`.
- `doesn't accept "<m>", but <c> sends it` → `accept "<m>"`; <c>: `stop sending "<m>" there`.

`<m>` is an enum value or a union member key, quoted, that the consumer declares and the provider doesn't, in a body either side produces. One block per value: the same value missing in two places is one block with ` (2 places)`, and two values of one field are two blocks. An `enum` reader against a `string` producer is a type break with the type `enum` (`sends it as string, but <c> expects enum`). The member lines:
  ```
  Pet.status — petstore_web reads "adopted", but petstore_api doesn't provide it
    → petstore_web: stop reading "adopted"
    → petstore_api: provide "adopted" there
      · GET /pets response 200 at "$[].status" (petstore_api: Pet.status)

  Pet.status — petstore_web sends "sold", but petstore_api doesn't accept it
    → petstore_web: stop sending "sold"
    → petstore_api: accept "sold" there
      · POST /pets request at "$.status" (petstore_api: Pet.status)
  ```

`rest` resource breaks come before any property is compared. In the report they print under `<METHOD> <endpoint>`, then `request:` or `response <s>:`, one break per line followed by its fix lines. Each, with the fix of the participant under check, then `<c>`'s:

- `calls <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> doesn't provide it` → `stop calling it`; <c>: `publish it`. The endpoint or method doesn't exist in <c>'s version deployed in <env>: check endpoint spelling (`*` segments) and method.
- `reads response <s>, but <c> answers only <statuses>` (`204`; `201 or 204`; `201, 204 or 404`) → `read response <statuses>`; <c>: `answer <s>`. Endpoint and method exist, that status doesn't.
- `reads response <s>, but <c> declares no response` → `stop reading it`; <c>: `answer <s>`.
- `sends a request body, but <c> declares none` → `stop sending it`; <c>: `accept a request body`. Endpoint and method exist with no `request`.
- A status only the provider declares obliges no one.
- `calls <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> is not deployed in <env>` → only <c>: `deploy it to <env> first`. <c> has no deployment in <env>, whatever it published: deployed elsewhere, never published, or not a participant. Check the provider name under `consumes`.
- `removed <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> still calls it` → `keep it until <c> stops calling it`; <c>: `stop calling it`. Printed once, right below `<METHOD> <endpoint>`, outside any `request` / `response <status>` group. Only when the endpoint and method are gone entirely; a dropped status or `request` on an endpoint and method that stay is one of the next three.
- `now answers <METHOD> <endpoint> only with <statuses>, but <c> still reads response <s>` → `keep answering <s> until <c> stops reading it`; <c>: `read response <statuses>`. Endpoint and method stay, that status is gone: `DELETE /pets/*` answering `204:` instead of `200: Pet` while <c> reads `200` is `now answers DELETE /pets/* only with 204, but <c> still reads response 200`.
- `no longer answers <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> still reads response <s>` → `keep answering <s> until <c> stops reading it`; <c>: `stop reading it`. Endpoint and method stay with no response at all.
- `dropped the request body of <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> still sends it` → `keep accepting it until <c> stops sending it`; <c>: `stop sending it`. Endpoint and method stay with no `request`.

`graphql` resource breaks print under `<operation> <field>` (`query pet`), one break per line followed by its fix lines:

- `calls <operation> <field>, but <c> doesn't provide it` → `stop calling it`; <c>: `publish it`.
- `calls <operation> <field>, but <c> is not deployed in <env>` → only <c>: `deploy it to <env> first` (a graph with no deployed subgraph: `deploy a subgraph of it to <env> first`, header `<graph>:`).
- `calls <operation> <field>, but <graph> can't be built in <env>: <cause>` → only `<graph> subgraphs: make it compose (see /graphs/<graph>)`.
- `removed <operation> <field>, but <c> still calls it` (in a subgraph's check `<participant> (via <graph>) removed …`) → `keep it until <c> stops calling it`; <c>: `stop calling it`.
- `<participant> (via <graph>) makes <graph> fail to compose in <env>: <cause>, and <c> calls <operation> <field>` → `make <graph> compose (see /graphs/<graph>)`.

`graphql` property breaks use the lines above with these differences: `reads it, but <c> doesn't provide it` → only `stop reading it`; in the arguments (also an argument of a nested field, placed under `returns` with `(argument "<a>")`), `sends it, but <c> doesn't accept it` → `stop sending it`; <c>: `accept it`, and `doesn't accept it, but <c> sends it` → `accept it`; <c>: `stop sending it`. Fields are GraphQL coordinates (`Pet.name`, `Query.pet(id:)`, `Pet.reviews(first:)`), the root place is `"$"`, and types print as GraphQL writes them (`[String!]!`, `Int`, `ID`, `DateTime!`, `enum (AVAILABLE | SOLD)!`).

Core rule, for every kind of resource: the side that reads a body decides what must be in it, and the provider owns how a property is provided. Which side produces depends on the resource (`rest`: a response is produced by the provider and read by the consumer, a request the reverse; `graphql`: `returns` is produced by the provider, `arguments` by the consumer). A property the reader requires must be declared by the producer, required too, with a type the reader accepts (the same type; a `number` reader also accepts `integer` and `float`; a `string` reader also accepts `enum`). Every enum value and union member the consumer declares must be declared by the provider, whichever side produces the body; one only the provider declares never breaks. A property is required only where its parent is present: when the producer does not declare a parent, only the parent can break (and only if it is required), nothing inside it is checked (array items and map values included). A property the reader marks optional may be absent, but if both declare it the reader must accept its type. A property the producer marks nullable must be nullable for the reader too. A property the reader does not declare is not checked.

## Docs

- [Overview](https://bidirekt.com/docs/README.md): what Bidirekt is, its CLI and its broker, and where to start.
- [Demo](https://bidirekt.com/docs/start/demo.md): the petstore demo step by step, from a `can-i-deploy` break to the fix.
- [Try on your project](https://bidirekt.com/docs/start/try.md): what `bidirekt.com/try` installs and the seven steps it prints.
- [Install](https://bidirekt.com/docs/start/install.md): the CLI with curl, with Homebrew, from the GitHub Release or as a Docker image, upgrading it, pointing it at a broker, and the agent skill.
- [Run the broker](https://bidirekt.com/docs/start/run-the-broker.md): the local Docker Compose broker, the broker with Homebrew and as a binary, upgrading it with a database backup, the admin created on the first access and its `local` profile signed in with `bidirekt login`, the broker image in production: its settings (`BIDIREKT_PUBLIC_URL`, `BIDIREKT_TRUSTED_PROXIES`, `BIDIREKT_TOKEN_SIGNING_KEY`), start-up checks, the admin, users and invite links, API keys (create on the Profile, permission, expiration, revoke), and the HTTPS reverse proxy, and the web UI: its pages, which every user reads, the graph page included, and creating participants and environments and renaming environments with `write`.
- [Why bidirectional](https://bidirekt.com/docs/concepts/why-bidirectional.md): what contract testing catches, consumer-driven vs provider-driven, and why both sides declare and nothing runs.
- [How the broker works](https://bidirekt.com/docs/concepts/how-the-broker-works.md): participant, environment, contract, version, snapshot, counterpart, can-i-deploy, deployment.
- [The contract file](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/the-contract-file.md): keys and resources, bodies not described, which side decides, describing what the code does, several files, what is not compared, file rules.
- [TypeScript SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/typescript-sdk.md): write the contract from TypeScript or JavaScript code with decorators (`@BidirektRestProvider`, `@BidirektRestConsumer`, `@BidirektGraphqlConsumer`, `@BidirektGraph`) or `@bidirekt` tags (`rest provides`, `rest consumes`, `graphql consumes`, `graph`): an example, the GraphQL consumer and graph, describing what the code does, the flow from `generate` to deploy, and `contracts/generated.yaml` as the service's contract, with the GraphQL schema for a subgraph; the full reference is the SDK's README.
- [PHP SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/php-sdk.md): write the contract from PHP code with attributes or `@bidirekt` docblock tags: an example, describing what the code does, the flow from `generate` to deploy, and `contracts/generated.yaml` as the service's only contract; the full reference is the SDK's README.
- [Go SDK](https://bidirekt.com/docs/contracts/go-sdk.md): write the contract from Go code with `bidirekt` declarations and struct tags: an example, describing what the code does, the flow from `generate` to deploy, and `contracts/generated.yaml` as the service's only contract; the full reference is the SDK's README.
- [Resources](https://bidirekt.com/docs/rest/resources.md): REST endpoints, requests, responses, which statuses to declare, `~` bodies, several files, what is not compared.
- [Resource breaks](https://bidirekt.com/docs/rest/breaks.md): the nine REST breaks that come before any property is compared, and their fixes.
- [GraphQL Resources](https://bidirekt.com/docs/graphql/resources.md): How a GraphQL provider publishes its schema, how a consumer declares the queries and mutations it calls, how GraphQL types become schemas and compare, the publish errors, and what a GraphQL contract does not compare.
- [GraphQL Breaks](https://bidirekt.com/docs/graphql/breaks.md): How the report shows a GraphQL break, the breaks of a field that come before any property is compared, the property breaks of GraphQL, and the fixes of each.
- [Graphs](https://bidirekt.com/docs/graphql/graphs.md): How subgraphs declare a federated graph, how the broker composes it in each environment, how a consumer of the graph and a subgraph are checked, what composition checks and does not check, the graph page, and the known gaps.
- [Types](https://bidirekt.com/docs/schemas/types.md): the node types, `scalar` included, the keys each takes, and how `integer`, `float` and `number` compare.
- [Optional and nullable](https://bidirekt.com/docs/schemas/optional-and-nullable.md): what each flag says and where it is accepted.
- [Objects](https://bidirekt.com/docs/schemas/objects.md): `properties`, and valid property and schema names.
- [Arrays and maps](https://bidirekt.com/docs/schemas/arrays-and-maps.md): `items`, `values`, and a map against an object.
- [Enums and unions](https://bidirekt.com/docs/schemas/enums-and-unions.md): `members` of an enum and of a union, what each rejects, and how the two sides compare them.
- [References](https://bidirekt.com/docs/schemas/references.md): `ref` to a named schema, recursion included, and the `ref` loop that is rejected.
- [validate](https://bidirekt.com/docs/ship/validate.md): check files before committing, and optionally compare them with an environment, without publishing.
- [publish](https://bidirekt.com/docs/ship/publish.md): publish files or folders as one version, and its errors.
- [can-i-deploy](https://bidirekt.com/docs/ship/can-i-deploy.md): ask whether a version can be deployed, and how to read the report.
- [Property breaks](https://bidirekt.com/docs/ship/property-breaks.md): every property break the report can print, with each side's fix.
- [record-deployment](https://bidirekt.com/docs/ship/record-deployment.md): record a deployment, rollbacks included.
- [CLI reference](https://bidirekt.com/docs/reference/cli.md): help output, broker address, config file, exit codes and output, every command.
